title: Early stage of development, suggestions for AI involvement
author: nebilim6
selftext:
**Table of content for this post**

1. Background
2. Why and how I started/keep developing the game
3. Tech stack
4. AI disclosure
5. Conclusion



*  **Background**

I am a software engineer, with 4-5 years of experience. I've worked in aviation/banking sectors so far, big enterprise systems that reach 100k-1M+ daily active users. I'm still working at a bank, for one of the corebanking departments.

I have experience in native mobile development (android & iOS), backend systems, web frontend technologies, and some devops. Simply put, I'm fullstack + additional skills.  


*  **Why and how I started/keep developing the game**

I have some prior game development experience from another web-based game project. It was for my self-entertainment and to learn new tech that I do not use regularly in my daily job. In the end, I feel I have taken my share of TypeScript shit and it's time to move on.

I'm a huge fan of management/colony simulation games. Every game I played did something very good but at some point either something felt missing or things got repetitive. So I decided to make one for myself to meet my needs as a gamer. Even if no one plays the game, it's fine, I can play myself. However, it would be nice if I could deliver it to some audience and maybe others can enjoy as well. 

The agreement with my current employer does not allow me to engage in additional financial activities anyway, so I'm not hoping for any income from this project, at least not anytime soon unless I resign, because I'd need a personal company to pay taxes.

* **Tech stack**

Language and Runtime: C# on .NET 10 (LTS) (until .NET 11 becomes stable enough)

Rendering: Raylib-cs (v7) for 2D drawings

The entire simulation is isolated into a backend DLL with zero external NuGet dependencies and the core has no awareness of graphics or rendering. Instead of pulling in a heavy third-party ECS library, I apply DOD (data oriented design) directly in pure C#. The entire world and colony overlays are stored as flat, contiguous arrays of value structs rather than deep object trees or multidimensional arrays. So, the logic is decoupled into stateless systems and dynamic data is referenced by lightweight IDs rather than heap-allocated object graphs. 

Why all the focus on performance?

Because I'm targeting a large-scale simulation where the world is actually alive. NPC settlements will produce goods using their own natural resources that replenish over time (no static shop refreshes out of thin air) and trade, fight, or engage in diplomacy based on their actual simulated needs. I'm also adding roaming bandit factions, beast lairs, and dynamic encounters so the world feels active beyond the player's borders.

* **AI Disclosure**

Well, this part is the main reason I'm posting this. I've already experienced the harsh resistance of anti-AI people in PBBG/idle game forums. The frustration is fair, to be honest, considering the flood of very similar-looking games with the same fonts, colors, and UI components. On the other hand, even when it's used well, it still gets instantly dismissed.

This is what I'd love to hear your opinions on: Where is the line to draw for limiting the usage of AI?

It appears to me that people care most about generative AI involvement when it comes to visual assets, rather than the coding itself. However, in the early stages; based on feedback, or when you get new ideas, or when you feel the need to refactor, replacing visual assets is much harder than refactoring the code, especially when you're doing both by yourself.

Even if I build a system that handles over 500 simulated settlers smoothly without FPS problems and delivers an engaging gameplay loop, does the gaming community still care if the code was AI-assisted or entirely generated, given that I actively supervise every line? Even when I write code completely by myself, reviewer agent will always find inefficiencies that need upgrading. But the second I hit that, the code is officially flagged for AI involvement and there's no return. 

I manage my codebase using different skill files regularly to plan, review, or do system-wide audits to ensure everything is consistent with my personal coding style and design principles. I have written custom service templates as reference models for the agents to follow. I avoid god-classes, prevent micro-files, keeping cognitive load low and there are clear JSDoc comments for everything. I can easily find and understand any function, regardless of whether an agent wrote it.

I also have domain-specific context files, engine/UI related guidance documents so that I can keep working as a human developer whenever I want, should there be an outage, no limit left, or simply for the personal satisfaction of writing code myself. When left unsupervised, no matter how intelligent the model is, it simply \*\*\*\*s up the whole architecture and folder organization. Leaving everything entirely to them is a terrible idea, but it's undeniable that working alongside them makes development vastly faster.

For art work it gets tricky. While items can share a base template PNG with material-based different colors baked in via code; drawing a proper cat from scratch would take hours for me, not to mention more complex animals/items. Because this is a side project that I work on during weekends and after my day job, my personal rest time is already limited. I would much rather spend it building actual game mechanics than struggling to draw sprites in Paint or whatever tool is meant for it.

* **Conclusion**

How to overcome this:

**Any AI involvement = lazy asset-flipping cash grab**

There should be a difference between someone pushing a single button to vomit out a generic asset-store clone and a solo developer who uses AI tools as a high-speed force multiplier. 

As I mentioned earlier, there is zero chance I'm making any money off this anytime soon anyway. My plan is likely to release a complete version as a stable demo, and if the time eventually comes to move on to next step, it will simply remain a stable platform that doesn't receive further updates.

I'd love to hear any opinion or answer any questions. Thanks in advance.
